Récolter, moissonner ; cueillir.

examples.text: Die Früchte wurden abgeerntet.

glosses: Récolter, moissonner (un champ, etc.).

examples.text: Um den Acker abzuernten, ist es schon zu dunkel.
examples.translation: Il fait déjà trop sombre pour moissonner le champ.

examples.text: Die abgeernteten Felder wurden (im Mittelalter) – nicht allein zum Vergnügen – bejagt, denn die Beutetiere waren wichtiger Bestandteil der Ernährung und versprachen Abwechslung auf der Speisekarte.
examples.translation: On pratiquait la chasse sur les champs moissonnés (au Moyen Âge), et pas seulement pour le plaisir, car les proies constituaient une part importante de l’alimentation et promettaient de varier les menus.

glosses: The process of gathering the ripened crop; harvesting.

examples.text: The constant rain made the harvest a nightmare this year.

glosses: The yield of harvesting, i.e., the gathered crops or fruits.

examples.text: This year's cotton harvest was great but the corn harvest was disastrous.

Hester Earle and Violet Wayne were moving about the aisle with bundles of wheat-ears and streamers of ivy, for the harvest thanksgiving was shortly to be celebrated, while the vicar stood waiting for their directions on the chancel steps with a great handful of crimson gladioli.

The frizzle-headed man-eaters were loath to leave their fleshpots so long as the harvest of human carcases was plentiful. Sometimes, when the harvest was too plentiful, they imposed on the missionaries by letting the word slip out that on such a day there would be a killing and a barbecue.
To glean the broken ears after the man / That the main harvest reaps.

glosses: The product or result of any exertion or course of action; reward or consequences.

examples.text: The surveillance mission yielded a healthy harvest of intel.
The pope's principal harvest was in the jubilee.
the harvest of a quiet eye

glosses: The season of gathering ripened crops; specifically, the time of reaping and gathering grain.
The third season of the year; autumn; fall.

examples.text: Harvest is usually very damp and rainy.

glosses: A modern pagan ceremony held on or around the autumn equinox, which is in the harvesting season.
To bring in a harvest; reap; glean.

examples.text: We harvested the apples in September already.

glosses: To take a living organism as part of a managed process to gather food or resources, often with the intention of maintaining a healthy population.

examples.text: An efficient rifle or shotgun can harvest a deer for venison.

glosses: To be occupied bringing in a harvest.

examples.text: We're going to harvest day and night, because the weather is about to turn sour.

glosses: To win, achieve a gain.

examples.text: The rising star harvested well-deserved acclaim, even an Oscar under 21.

glosses: A tool used for digging; a pickaxe.
An anchor.

examples.text: It's better to amble around, drop the "pick" for a lunchtime swim or beachcomb, then find a nice anchorage for the night.

glosses: A pointed hammer used for dressing millstones.
A tool for unlocking a lock without the original key; a lock pick, picklock.
A comb with long widely spaced teeth, for use with tightly curled hair.
A tool used for strumming the strings of a guitar; a plectrum.
A pike or spike; the sharp point fixed in the center of a buckler.

examples.text: Take down my buckler […] and grind the pick on 't.

glosses: A choice; ability to choose.

examples.text: France and Russia have the pick of our stables.

glosses: That which would be picked or chosen first; the best.
Pasture; feed, for animals.

examples.text: ‘She's all African grass and Brahmans. There's not a blade of native pick left, except on the ridges.’

The judicious use of fire could have protected valuable nut trees, promoted the growth and seeding of grass and, if practised at a distance from their camps, even attracted herbivores to the sweet young pick.

glosses: A screen.
An offensive tactic in which a player stands so as to block a defender from reaching a teammate.
An interception.
A good defensive play by an infielder.
A pickoff.
A particle of ink or paper embedded in the hollow of a letter, filling up its face, and causing a spot on a printed sheet.

examples.text: If it be in the smallest degree gritty, it clogs the form, and consequently produces a thick and imperfect impression; no pains should, therefore, be spared to render it perfectly smooth; it may then be made to work as clear and free from picks

glosses: That which is picked in, as with a pointed pencil, to correct an unevenness in a picture.
The blow that drives the shuttle, used in calculating the speed of a loom (in picks per minute); hence, in describing the fineness of a fabric, a weft thread.

examples.text: so many picks to an inch

glosses: To grasp and pull with the fingers or fingernails.

examples.text: Don't pick at that scab.
He picked his nose.

glosses: To harvest a fruit or vegetable for consumption by removing it from the plant to which it is attached; to harvest an entire plant by removing it from the ground.

examples.text: It's time to pick the tomatoes.

glosses: To pull apart or away, especially with the fingers; to pluck.

examples.text: She picked flowers in the meadow.
to pick feathers from a fowl

glosses: To take up; especially, to gather from here and there; to collect; to bring together.

examples.text: to pick rags

glosses: To remove something from somewhere with a pointed instrument, with the fingers, or with the teeth.

examples.text: to pick the teeth; to pick a bone; to pick a goose; to pick a pocket
Did you pick Master Slender's purse?
He picks clean teeth, and, busy as he seems / With an old tavern quill, is hungry yet.
He was charged with attempting to pick a pocket, and they found a silver snuff-box on him,--his own, my dear, his own, for he took snuff himself, and was very fond of it.
For the pocket in which Erskine kept this key was not the kind of pocket that Watt could pick. For it was no ordinary pocket, no, but a secret one, sewn on to the front of Erskine's underhose.

glosses: To decide upon, from a set of options; to select.

examples.text: I'll pick the one with the nicest name.

glosses: To seek (a fight or quarrel) where the opportunity arises.
To recognise the type of ball being bowled by a bowler by studying the position of the hand and arm as the ball is released.

examples.text: He didn't pick the googly, and was bowled.

glosses: To pluck the individual strings of a musical instrument or to play such an instrument.

examples.text: He picked a tune on his banjo.

glosses: To open (a lock) with a wire, lock pick, etc.

examples.text: The lock was of a kind that Watt could not pick. Watt could pick simple locks, but he could not pick obscure locks.

glosses: To eat slowly, sparingly, or by morsels; to nibble.

examples.text: Why stand'st thou picking? Is thy palate sore?

glosses: To do anything fastidiously or carefully, or by attending to small things; to select something with care.

examples.text: I gingerly picked my way between the thorny shrubs.

glosses: To steal; to pilfer.

examples.text: to keep my hands from picking and stealing

glosses: To throw; to pitch.

examples.text: as high as I could pick my lance

glosses: To peck at, as a bird with its beak; to strike at with anything pointed; to act upon with a pointed instrument; to pierce; to prick, as with a pin.
To separate or open by means of a sharp point or points.

examples.text: to pick matted wool, cotton, oakum, etc.
Naphtha lamps shed a weird light over a busy scene, for the work was being continued night and day. A score or so of sturdy navvies were shovelling and picking along the track.

glosses: To screen.
To intercept a pass from the offense as a defensive player.

examples.text: The pass was almost picked, but the tight end was able to hold on.

glosses: Faucher et récolter les blés et autres céréales.

examples.text: Les paysans qui moissonnaient se retrouvaient le dimanche transformés en acteurs pour des familles pique-niquantes, étonnées du spectacle.

glosses: Recevoir, récolter.

examples.text: Moissonner des palmes, des lauriers.

glosses: Faucher, détruire, faire périr.

examples.text: Combien de personnes, dans l’espèce humaine, ne voit-on pas moissonnées avant l’âge par le manque d’exercice fonctionnel !
Les épidémies ont moissonné une grande partie de la population.
Une vie qui s’annonçait si belle a été moissonnée dans sa fleur.

glosses: Recueillir des informations à partir d’une recherche méthodique.
tags: Sciences de l’information et de la communication

examples.text: […] ainsi qu’une loi sur l’information technique japonaise pour entraîner le pays entier à moissonner cette information.

glosses: Détacher des fruits, des fleurs, des légumes de leurs branches ou de leurs tiges.

examples.text: Les deux couples riaient, bavardaient, cueillaient des fleurs, se cajolaient et se mignotaient, luttaient et se roulaient sur l’herbe, et les jeunes filles fumèrent des cigarettes.

Il était allé lui cueillir un bouquet de coucous pour mettre au pied de la statue de la Vierge qui trônait sur un vieux confiturier reconverti en fourre-tout de laines et de tissus où elle puisait pour occuper ses doigts.

— On avait cueilli autour de l’église et dans le cimetière. Maigrement fruités les arbres donnèrent moins d’une demi-hottée chacun ; mais quelle graine ! Nourrie du suc des Trépassés, ronde comme une prunelle.
Cueillir des palmes, cueillir des lauriers, remporter des succès, des victoires.

glosses: Prendre.

examples.text: Cueillir un baiser sur les lèvres de sa bien aimée.
Ce fut, en ce temps de relative splendeur, qu’un soir de bombe, à Montparnasse, il cueillit Geneviève à une table de café.
Cueille ce triste jour d’hiver sur la mer grise

glosses: Arrêter un coupable par surprise au moment où il se croyait hors d’atteinte.

examples.text: Comme on l’avait à l’œil pour un vol de soieries, on a été le cueillir doucement à la sortie du spectacle.

glosses: Se faire frapper par surprise à la boxe.

examples.text: Kravine a dopé son mec. Deux reprises et je le cueille.
Il était sur le point de prendre une arme dans une commode quand Oscar l’a cueilli comme une marguerite.

glosses: Faire une récolte.

examples.text: Un bon terrain peut fournir jusqu’à cent milliers de betteraves par hectare, j’en ai même récolté jusqu’à cent vingt sur un pré nouvellement défriché, […].

glosses: Gagner par son labeur.

examples.text: […] Sébastien Chambot […] qui récolte des paquets de billets de mille avec des romans alambiqués et voluptueux, où il n'est question que de tortillements de la viande humaine saturée de cantharide.

glosses: Recevoir en retour.

examples.text: Il n’y a récolté que des coups. — Il a récolté ce qu'il méritait.

L’entreprise ajoute qu’elle pourra aussi récolter des données n’appartenant pas à des utilisateurs de ses services : « Par exemple, cela peut être le cas si vous apparaissez sur une image partagée par un·e utilisateur·ice sur nos produits ou services ou si une personne mentionne des informations vous concernant dans des messages ou des légendes partagées sur nos produits et services. »
